sections.h2: Does New Hampshire have an estate tax or inheritance tax?
sections.html:
No. New Hampshire repealed its inheritance tax (the Legacy and Succession Tax) for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, and its separate state estate tax return is no longer required for deaths on or after January 1, 2005.

The Department of Revenue Administration (DRA) explains the second step this way: the state estate tax depended on a federal credit, and when the federal estate death tax credit was repealed, the NH Estate Tax return was no longer required. A third tax, the transfer tax on personal property of nonresident decedents (RSA 89), was repealed for the same 2003 deaths.

For an heir deciding whether to sell an inherited New Hampshire house, that means no state death tax bill sits between you and the sale. Other costs still apply, and they are covered below.

sections.h2: What did the old New Hampshire death taxes look like?
sections.html:
The old Legacy and Succession Tax was an inheritance tax that fell on certain heirs, not on the estate as a whole. It only matters now if you are dealing with a death before 2003, which is rare but possible in a long-unsettled estate.

TaxStatusApplies to deaths
Legacy and Succession Tax (RSA 86)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
Transfer tax on nonresident decedents' personal property (RSA 89)RepealedOn or after January 1, 2003
NH Estate Tax return (NH-706)Not requiredOn or after January 1, 2005

Under the old rules, the DRA says a tax return was due nine months from the date of death. Spouses, children, parents, grandparents and grandchildren were among the non-taxable legatees. Brothers, sisters, nieces, nephews, friends and other non-relatives were among the taxable ones. The old NH-706 filing threshold was $675,000 for deaths in 2000 and 2001 and $1,000,000 for 2002 through 2004.

sections.h2: Does the federal estate tax matter for a house sale?
sections.html:
Only for large estates. The IRS lists the basic exclusion amount for a 2026 death at $15,000,000, and that is also the filing threshold for an estate tax return for a 2026 death.

The IRS lists the annual gift tax exclusion for 2026 gifts at $19,000 per donee. An estate whose gross value falls below the exclusion generally has no federal estate tax to pay, so most New Hampshire families selling a parent's house are not affected.

  • Check the date of death, because the exclusion amount is set by year of death.
  • Add up the whole estate, not just the house.
  • If the estate is near the threshold, ask an estate attorney before you sell.

sections.h2: What taxes can an heir still owe when selling an inherited New Hampshire house?
sections.html:
The main ones are the state real estate transfer tax on the sale, property tax, and possibly federal income tax on gain. The transfer into your name is a different matter: the DRA says transfers by devise, intestate succession, or the death of a joint tenant are exempt from the real estate transfer tax.

The sale itself is taxed. The transfer tax is $0.75 per $100 of the price, paid by both buyer and seller, with a $20 minimum each for a price of $4,000 or less. Buyer and seller purchase stamps from the register of deeds in the property's county.

Within 30 days after the deed is recorded, the state expects the purchaser's and seller's declarations of consideration and an Inventory of Property Transfer (PA-34).

  1. Transfer tax on the sale, for the seller's half
  2. Unpaid property tax and any recorded lien
  3. Federal capital gain tax, if the sale price is above your basis (see our capital gains guide)

The IRS directs people who inherit property to Publication 551 for their basis rules, so ask your preparer how it applies to this house.

sections.h2: How does probate affect selling an inherited house in New Hampshire?
sections.html:
The estate's executor or administrator is the person who normally sells, and the Circuit Court Probate Division supervises. The DRA tells people with questions about probating an estate to contact the Probate Court in the county where the decedent lived.

The court's booklet, Administering an Estate, says an executor is named in a will and an administrator is appointed when there is no named executor. It tells the person in charge to try to get the best price when real estate or personal property is sold. The Judicial Branch also provides a Motion and License to Sell Real Estate to Pay Demands, used when an executor or administrator wants a license to sell the property to pay debts or claims against the estate.

When the work is done, the executor files a final accounting on the Executor's/Administrator's Accounting form (NHJB-2117-Pe) so that the duties can be released.

Our New Hampshire probate guide covers the court steps in more detail.

sections.h2: Who pays the property tax on an inherited house while the estate is open?
sections.html:
The property keeps being taxed in the meantime, and the estate or the heir who holds it is responsible for the bill. New Hampshire's tax year runs April 1 to March 31 (RSA 76:2), so a house can generate two bills while probate is still pending.

Unpaid tax carries 8 percent interest under RSA 76:13. Once a lien is recorded, RSA 80:69 allows anyone with a legal interest in the land to redeem it by paying the lien amount with interest at 14 percent per year before the collector gives a deed.

  • File a change of mailing address with the town or city assessing office.
  • Ask the tax collector for a current payoff before listing.
  • Note that a new deed can take 30 days or more to reach the assessing office after a transfer, according to Manchester's tax collector.

sections.h2: Where can you get official answers about death taxes in New Hampshire?
sections.html:
Call the DRA Taxpayer Services Call Center at (603) 230-5920 for state questions, or write to NH DRA, Estate & Legacy, PO Box 457, Concord, NH 03302-0457. The DRA's inheritance and estate tax pages are the place to confirm that no state return is needed for a recent death.

For federal questions, the IRS estate tax page lists the filing threshold by year of death, and its Form 706 instructions explain the return for estates that exceed it. For the court side, the Probate Division of the Circuit Court handles wills, trusts and estates, and the county where the decedent lived decides where the case is filed.

Keep every answer in writing. A title company will want to see that the estate has authority to sell and that taxes and liens are cleared before it closes.

sections.h2: What are your options if you inherited a New Hampshire house you do not want?
sections.html:
You can keep it, rent it, sell it on the open market, or sell it as-is to a cash buyer. The tax picture above stays the same for each, and the differences are in time and repair cost.

An as-is cash sale can suit an estate with a house that needs work, back taxes or out-of-state heirs, because the buyer pays for the property in its present condition and the title company settles taxes and liens at closing. We make no promise about price here, since every house and every town is different.

Before choosing, gather the death certificate, the will or court appointment papers, the latest tax bill, and any lien notices.

faqs.q: Does New Hampshire have an inheritance tax?
faqs.a: No. The Legacy and Succession Tax was repealed for deaths on or after January 1, 2003, according to the DRA.

faqs.q: Is there a New Hampshire estate tax return to file?
faqs.a: Not for deaths on or after January 1, 2005. The DRA says the NH Estate Tax return is not required because the federal estate death tax credit was repealed.

faqs.q: Do I pay transfer tax when a house passes to me by will?
faqs.a: No. The DRA lists transfers by devise, intestate succession and the death of a joint tenant as exempt. A later sale by you is taxed at $0.75 per $100, split between buyer and seller.

faqs.q: What is the federal estate tax threshold in 2026?
faqs.a: $15,000,000 for a 2026 death, according to the IRS. Estates below that amount generally do not owe federal estate tax.

faqs.q: Who handles questions about probate in New Hampshire?
faqs.a: The Probate Court in the county where the decedent lived, part of the Circuit Court Probate Division. The DRA directs probate questions there.
